claim: Large-scale multi-photon imaging and holographic stimulation offers the ability to accurately track and record from the same neuronal populations over extended periods at high spatiotemporal resolution.
source: Large-scale multi-photon imaging and holographic stimulation offers the ability to accurately track and record from the same neuronal populations over extended periods at high spatiotemporal resolution, record from axons, dendrites, and dendritic spines, and stimulate neurons with single-cell precision (Bando et al., 2021; Chaigneau et al., 2016; Dombeck et al., 2010; Dong et al., 2021; Emiliani et al., 2015; Fan et al., 2023; Hattori and Komiyama, 2022; Heer and Sheffield, 2024; Hernandez et al., 2016; Krishnan et al., 2022; Russell et al., 2022; Sheffield and Dombeck, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work demonstrating these capabilities.

claim: Large-scale multi-photon imaging and holographic stimulation enables recording from axons, dendrites, and dendritic spines.
source: Large-scale multi-photon imaging and holographic stimulation offers the ability to accurately track and record from the same neuronal populations over extended periods at high spatiotemporal resolution, record from axons, dendrites, and dendritic spines, and stimulate neurons with single-cell precision (Bando et al., 2021; Chaigneau et al., 2016; Dombeck et al., 2010; Dong et al., 2021; Emiliani et al., 2015; Fan et al., 2023; Hattori and Komiyama, 2022; Heer and Sheffield, 2024; Hernandez et al., 2016; Krishnan et al., 2022; Russell et al., 2022; Sheffield and Dombeck, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Large-scale multi-photon imaging and holographic stimulation enables stimulation of neurons with single-cell precision.
source: Large-scale multi-photon imaging and holographic stimulation offers the ability to accurately track and record from the same neuronal populations over extended periods at high spatiotemporal resolution, record from axons, dendrites, and dendritic spines, and stimulate neurons with single-cell precision (Bando et al., 2021; Chaigneau et al., 2016; Dombeck et al., 2010; Dong et al., 2021; Emiliani et al., 2015; Fan et al., 2023; Hattori and Komiyama, 2022; Heer and Sheffield, 2024; Hernandez et al., 2016; Krishnan et al., 2022; Russell et al., 2022; Sheffield and Dombeck, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Multi-photon imaging and holographic stimulation techniques generally require animals to be head-fixed.
source: However, head-fixation of animals, which is generally required to utilize these techniques, imposes constraints on the range of testable behaviors compared to freely moving conditions (Guo et al., 2014; Juczewski et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Head-fixation imposes constraints on the range of testable behaviors compared to freely moving conditions.
source: However, head-fixation of animals, which is generally required to utilize these techniques, imposes constraints on the range of testable behaviors compared to freely moving conditions (Guo et al., 2014; Juczewski et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Contextual fear conditioning is a laboratory method for testing associative learning, fear memory formation, and recall.
source: This limitation is particularly evident in the Pavlovian CFC task, a laboratory method for testing associative learning, fear memory formation, and recall (Bouton, 1993; Fanselow, 1980; Fanselow, 1990; Kim and Fanselow, 1992; LeDoux, 2000; Maren, 2001; Maren et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In traditional CFC paradigm, an animal is placed in an environment (conditioned stimulus, CS) that is paired with an aversive stimulus such as a mild foot shock (unconditioned stimulus, US).
source: In the traditional CFC paradigm for freely moving animals, an animal is placed in an environment (conditioned stimulus, CS) that is paired with an aversive stimulus, such as a mild foot shock (unconditioned stimulus, US).
evidence: The claim describes the standard CFC protocol, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: When reintroduced to the shock-paired environment, animals exhibit freezing behavior in rodents if they successfully associate the environment with the aversive stimulus.
source: When reintroduced to the environment, animals exhibit a species-specific conditioned response, such as fearful freezing behavior in rodents, if they successfully associate the shock-paired environment with the aversive stimulus.
evidence: The claim describes the standard behavioral response in CFC, which is established knowledge.

claim: The CFC paradigm is one of the most basic conditioning procedures for freely moving animals—it's simple and robust.
source: The CFC paradigm is one of the most basic conditioning procedures for freely moving animals— it's simple and robust (Fanselow, 1980; Fanselow, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Two prior studies reported a version of CFC in head-fixed mice with aversive air puffs as the US.
source: Two prior studies (Lovett-Barron et al., 2014; Rajasethupathy et al., 2015) reported a version of CFC in head-fixed mice with aversive air puffs as the US.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to specific prior studies.

claim: Prior head-fixed CFC studies reported the conditioned response as lick suppression, not freezing.
source: These studies reported the conditioned response animals displayed as lick suppression, not freezing.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to prior studies (Lovett-Barron et al., 2014; Rajasethupathy et al., 2015).

claim: Lick suppression after fear conditioning has been shown to result from increased freezing.
source: Although lick suppression after fear conditioning has also been observed in freely moving animals (Leaf and Leaf, 1966; Leaf and Muller, 1965), it has been shown to result from increased freezing (Bouton and Bolles, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Head-fixed mice were trained to run on a treadmill and navigate VR environments for water rewards.
source: To establish the contextual fear conditioning protocol (Figure 1A–C), head-fixed mice were water-restricted and trained to run on a treadmill and navigate VR environments for water rewards, as we have demonstrated previously (Dong et al., 2021; Krishnan et al., 2022; Krishnan and Sheffield, 2023; Ratigan et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors and describes the training protocol used.

claim: Forward movement on the treadmill translates to forward movement in VR, allowing mice to navigate the VR environment.
source: Forward movement on the treadmill translates to forward movement in VR, allowing mice to navigate the VR environment.
evidence: The claim describes the technical setup of the VR system.

claim: The VR environments used were 2m-long linear tracks rich in visual cues.
source: The environments used were 2m-long linear tracks rich in visual cues (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and Figure 1 showing the VR environments.

claim: Reaching the track's end triggered a water reward and defined a completed trial/lap.
source: Reaching the track's end triggered a water reward and defined a completed trial/lap.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Head-fixed mice placed on a treadmill do not automatically start exploring VR environments.
source: Unlike freely moving mice that tend to explore new environments, head-fixed mice placed on a treadmill do not automatically start exploring VR environments.
evidence: The claim describes an observed behavioral difference between freely moving and head-fixed mice.

claim: Head-fixed mice can be trained to explore VR environments through reinforcement learning using water restriction and water rewards.
source: However, they can be trained through reinforcement learning using water restriction and water rewards (Dombeck et al., 2010; Dong et al., 2021; Krishnan et al., 2022; Ratigan et al., 2023; Sheffield and Dombeck, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Training to navigate VR environments on a treadmill using water rewards was achieved in approximately 10–14 days.
source: Training to navigate VR environments on a treadmill (Stage 1), using water rewards, was achieved in approximately 10–14 d, after which well-trained mice could run several laps per minute.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the training protocol described in the manuscript.

claim: A criterion of >3 laps per minute was set for mice to advance to the next stage.
source: We set a criterion of >3 laps per minute (i.e. a lap velocity of 0.1–0.2 m/s) for mice to move on to the next stage (Stage 2).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol.

claim: When the tail-coat was added, some mice reduced their running speed or refused to move.
source: When the tail-coat was added, some mice reduced their running speed or refused to move.
evidence: The claim describes observed behavioral responses during the experiment.

claim: Approximately 20% of mice failed to meet the running speed criterion after tail-coat addition.
source: Some recovered the next day, but if their running speed did not reach at least three laps per minute (~20% of mice failed to meet this criterion), they were not advanced to the next stage.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the experimental protocol.

claim: Around 40% of mice dropped out when water reward was removed while wearing the tail-coat.
source: Mice that continued to run at least three laps per minute with the tail-coat and without water reward advanced to the experiment stage (Stage 4). Around 40% of the mice dropped out at this stage.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the experimental protocol.

claim: About 40% of mice proceeded to the experimental stage after meeting all training criteria.
source: This threshold resulted in about 40% of the mice proceeding to the experimental stage.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the experimental protocol.

claim: Once mice qualified for the experimental stage, they were no longer excluded from analysis due to their behavior.
source: Once mice qualified for the experimental stage, they were no longer excluded from analysis due to their behavior.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol and analysis criteria.

claim: In Paradigm 1, the neutral environment was the training VR environment, and a new VR environment was paired with shocks.
source: In Paradigm 1, the neutral environment was the training VR environment, and a new VR environment was paired with shocks.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design of Paradigm 1.

claim: In Paradigms 2 and 3, both the neutral and shock-paired environments were new and distinct from the training environment.
source: In Paradigms 2 and 3, both the neutral and shock-paired environments were new and distinct from the training environment to better control for environmental familiarity.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design of Paradigms 2 and 3.

claim: In Paradigms 1 and 2, the tail-coat was removed on the days following CFC.
source: In Paradigms 1 and 2, the tail-coat was removed on the days following CFC, whereas in Paradigm 3, it remained on the mouse on all post-CFC days.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol differences between paradigms.

claim: In Paradigm 3, the tail-coat remained on the mouse on all post-CFC days.
source: In Paradigms 1 and 2, the tail-coat was removed on the days following CFC, whereas in Paradigm 3, it remained on the mouse on all post-CFC days.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol of Paradigm 3.

claim: In Paradigm 1, 27 mice (25 males and 2 females) were used.
source: On Day 0 of the experimental stage in Paradigm 1 (CFC day), mice (n=27, 25 males and 2 females) were exposed to the same VR environment we used for training, referred to as the Familiar VR from here onwards (Figure 1C), for 10 min.
evidence: The claim describes the sample size and composition.

claim: Mice received 4–12 shocks at 0.5-1 mA amplitude, 1 s long, in the CFC VR.
source: Following baseline exploration of the CFC VR for 10 min, we repeatedly applied mild-electric shocks (4–12 shocks, 0.5-1 mA in amplitude, 1 s long) to the mouse's tail.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Shocks were pseudo-randomly administered with respect to the animal's position in the CFC VR, with an inter-shock interval (ISI) of 1 min.
source: Shocks were pseudo-randomly administered with respect to the animal's position in the CFC VR, with an inter-shock interval (ISI) of 1 min.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol.

claim: An immediate increase in running speed was observed following each shock.
source: We quantified the animal's response to the shocks and observed an immediate increase in running speed following each shock (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The immediate increase in running speed following shock was consistent across all mice and shocks.
source: This was consistent across all mice and shocks and was a reliable indicator that the apparatus was working correctly.
evidence: The claim is based on observed data across all experimental subjects.

claim: Before fear conditioning, mice exhibited similar behavior in both the Familiar and CFC VRs.
source: Before fear conditioning, mice exhibited similar behavior in both the Familiar and CFC VRs. We evaluated the time taken to complete a lap and the freezing behavior (defined as time points when the animal's instantaneous velocity was 0 cm/s). Neither metric revealed a significant difference between the two VRs before shock administration (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: After CFC, mice showed a significant increase in freezing in the CFC VR compared to the Familiar VR on recall Day 1.
source: However, after CFC, when the animals were reintroduced to the VRs on recall Day 1, we observed a significant increase in freezing and time taken to complete a lap in the CFC VR compared to the Familiar VR (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A–D.

claim: After CFC, mice showed a significant increase in time taken to complete a lap in the CFC VR compared to the Familiar VR on recall Day 1.
source: However, after CFC, when the animals were reintroduced to the VRs on recall Day 1, we observed a significant increase in freezing and time taken to complete a lap in the CFC VR compared to the Familiar VR (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A–D.

claim: Mice displayed behaviors such as slowing down, freezing, moving backward, and hesitation to move forward when transitioning to the CFC VR on recall day.
source: As soon as mice transitioned to the CFC VR (either from dark or after the Familiar VR) on the recall day, we observed behaviors such as slowing down, freezing, moving backward, and hesitation to move forward (Videos 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by video evidence (Videos 1–3).

claim: The difference in behavior between Familiar VR and CFC VR can be observed clearly in most mice on the very first lap.
source: This difference in behavior can be observed clearly in most mice on the very first lap (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A–B.

claim: Average freezing percentage on recall day was 17.52±3.25% in Familiar VR and 23.54±3.26% in CFC VR (p=0.001, n=27).
source: When we quantified the freezing behavior in mice, we found it to be, on average, high throughout the 5 min that mice spent in the CFC VR on recall Day 1 (Figure 2C–D, average freezing (%), mean ± 95% Confidence Intervals (CI), Familiar VR: 17.52±3.25, CFC VR: 23.54±3.26, p=0.001, Paired t-test, n=27).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2C–D.

claim: First lap freezing percentage was 15.94±4.03% in Familiar VR and 25.11±3.41% in CFC VR (p<0.001).
source: We also observed a significant increase in freezing during the first lap in the CFC VR compared to the familiar VR (Figure 2B–C, average first lap freezing (%), Familiar VR: 15.94±4.03, CFC VR: 25.11±3.41, p<0.001, Paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2B–C.

claim: Average time taken to complete first lap was 14.81±3.74 s in Familiar VR and 41.16±9.33 s in CFC VR (p<0.001).
source: Mice also took longer to complete a lap in the CFC VR compared to the Familiar VR, both in the first lap (average time taken to complete first lap (s), Familiar VR: 14.81±3.74, CFC VR: 41.16±9.33, p<0.001, Paired t-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Average time taken to complete all laps was 16.17±3.05 s in Familiar VR and 38.82±11.06 s in CFC VR (p<0.001).
source: and on average (Figure 2E–F, the average time taken to complete all laps (s), Familiar VR: 16.17±3.05, CFC VR: 38.82±11.06, p<0.001, Paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2E–F.

claim: The majority of mice (7/12) displayed appropriate memory recall at 1 mA intensity and six shocks.
source: The majority of mice (7/12) displayed appropriate memory recall (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B), indicated by more freezing in the CFC VR compared to the Familiar VR (delta >0), while 3/12 mice froze more in the Familiar VR (delta <0), and 2/12 showed equal freezing levels in both VRs (delta ≈ 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Variability in fear conditioning responses has been regularly documented in freely moving animals.
source: Such variability has been regularly documented in freely moving animals and may not be unique to the VR setup used here (Chu et al., 2024; Dos Santos Corrêa et al., 2019; Navarro-Sánchez et al., 2024; Poulos et al., 2016; Russo and Parsons, 2021; Totty et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Increasing the shock amplitude from 0.6 to 1 mA significantly enhanced both fear discrimination and freezing behavior.
source: Notably, increasing the shock amplitude from 0.6 to 1 mA, while keeping the number of shocks consistent at 6 shocks, significantly enhanced both fear discrimination and freezing behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: Fear discrimination was most prominent on Recall Day 1.
source: Fear discrimination was most prominent on Recall Day 1. Mice displayed the most substantial increase in freezing in the CFC VR compared to the Familiar VR on Recall Day 1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F–G.

claim: Freezing on the first lap in the CFC VR was most pronounced on Recall Day 1.
source: Freezing on the first lap in the CFC VR was also most pronounced on Recall Day 1.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental data across recall days.

claim: In the CFC VR, both first lap and average freezing were most prominent on Recall Day 1 and returned to baseline levels by Recall Day 2.
source: In the CFC VR, both first lap and average freezing were most prominent on Recall Day 1 and returned to baseline levels by Recall Day 2.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis using Linear Mixed Effects Model (Tables 1–2).

claim: In Paradigm 2, mice showed no differences in licking behavior across all experimental sessions in the novel VRs.
source: Compared to Paradigm 1, in the novel VRs, mice showed no differences in licking behavior across all experimental sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was no significant difference in freezing behavior and time taken to complete a lap between the two VRs on Day –1 and Day 0 before fear conditioning in Paradigm 2.
source: There was also no significant difference in freezing behavior and time taken to complete a lap between the two VRs on Day –1 and Day 0 before fear conditioning (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: First lap freezing in the CFC VR was markedly higher in Paradigm 2 compared to Paradigm 1.
source: While first lap freezing in the CFC VR was markedly higher in Paradigm 2, significant differences between the Control VR and CFC VR were observed only for first lap freezing, not for average freezing or lap completion time across all laps (Figures 3B–D–4A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3B–D and 4A–E.

claim: In Paradigm 2, significant differences between the Control VR and CFC VR were observed only for first lap freezing, not for average freezing or lap completion time across all laps.
source: While first lap freezing in the CFC VR was markedly higher in Paradigm 2, significant differences between the Control VR and CFC VR were observed only for first lap freezing, not for average freezing or lap completion time across all laps (Figures 3B–D–4A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3B–D and 4A–E.

claim: The effect sizes for the difference in first lap freezing between the two VRs were nearly identical between Paradigm 1 and Paradigm 2 (Cohen's d: Paradigm 1: 1.038, Paradigm 2: 1.040).
source: The effect sizes for the difference in first lap freezing between the two VRs were nearly identical between the paradigms (Cohen's d: First lap freezing: Paradigm 1: 1.038, Paradigm 2: 1.040)
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The effect size for average freezing was notably smaller in Paradigm 2 compared to Paradigm 1 (Cohen's d: Paradigm 1: 0.797, Paradigm 2: 0.093).
source: but the effect size for average freezing was notably smaller in Paradigm 2 compared to Paradigm 1 (Cohen's d: Average Freezing: Paradigm 1: 0.797, Paradigm 2: 0.093).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Paradigm 2, after the first lap, mice showed similar freezing in both the Control VR and the CFC VR across all subsequent laps on Recall Day 1.
source: When we quantified freezing by lap on Recall Day 1 in Paradigm 2, we found that after the first lap, mice showed similar freezing in both the Control VR and the CFC VR across all subsequent laps (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Paradigm 1, mice consistently froze more in the CFC VR compared to the Familiar VR throughout Recall Day 1.
source: In contrast, in Paradigm 1, mice consistently froze more in the CFC VR compared to the Familiar VR throughout Recall Day 1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Paradigm 2, freezing in first lap was 11.04±1.8% in Control VR and 16.05±3.94% in CFC VR (p=0.016).
source: Indeed, when we quantified freezing behavior in the Control VR and CFC VR in Paradigm 2, we found that the most significant increase in freezing and other avoidance-like defensive behaviors in the CFC VR was observed in the first lap (freezing in first lap %: Control VR: 11.04±1.8 CFC VR: 16.05±3.94, p=0.016
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Paradigm 2, time taken to complete first lap was 14.27±2.85 s in Control VR and 25.68±5.55 s in CFC VR (p=0.001).
source: time taken to complete first lap (s): Control VR: 14.27±2.85, CFC VR: 25.68±5.55, p=0.001, Paired t-test, Figure 3B–E, Figure 4A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 3B–E and 4A–E.

claim: In Paradigm 2, average freezing in all laps was 20.54±4.13% in Control VR and 21.15±4.21% in CFC VR (p=0.738).
source: Neither average freezing across all laps (Figure 4C, average freezing in all laps %: Control VR: 20.54±4.13, CFC VR: 21.15±4.21, p=0.738, Paired t-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In Paradigm 2, average time taken to complete all laps was 21.73±8.11 s in Control VR and 24.27±6.36 s in CFC VR (p=0.558).
source: nor time taken to complete all laps (Figure 4E, the average time taken to complete all laps: Control VR: 21.73±8.11, CFC VR: 24.27±6.36, p=0.558, Paired t-test) showed significant differences between the two VRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In Paradigm 2, fear extinction occurs rapidly within the first recall session after the initial lap.
source: Thus, in Paradigm 2, fear extinction occurs rapidly within the first recall session after the initial lap.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of freezing data across recall days (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–D, Tables 3–4).

claim: In Paradigm 3, mice showed better fear discrimination between the Control and CFC VRs compared to Paradigm 2.
source: We found that mice (n=20 male mice) showed better fear discrimination between the Control and CFC VRs in Paradigm 3 compared to Paradigm 2 (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: In Paradigm 3, mice showed significant freezing in the first lap (Control VR: 13.61±2.24%, CFC VR: 19.73±5.17%, p=0.021).
source: Mice not only showed significant freezing in the first lap (freezing in first lap %: Control VR: 13.61±2.24 CFC VR: 19.73±5.17, p=0.021, Paired t-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Paradigm 3, average freezing across all laps was higher in the CFC VR compared to the Control VR (Control VR: 15.28±2.00%, CFC VR: 21.92±2.95%, p<0.001).
source: but average freezing across all laps was also higher in the CFC VR compared to the Control VR (Figure 5C–D, Figure 6A–D, average freezing in all laps %: Control VR: 15.28±2.00, CFC VR: 21.92±2.95, p<0.001, Paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 5C–D and 6A–D.

claim: Paradigm 3 showed a weaker effect size for first lap freezing compared to Paradigms 1 and 2 (Cohen's d: Paradigm 1: 1.038, Paradigm 2: 1.040, Paradigm 3: 0.719).
source: While first lap freezing showed a weaker effect size in Paradigm 3 compared to the other paradigms, there was a strong effect of average freezing across the session (Cohen's d: First lap freezing: Paradigm 1: 1.038, Paradigm 2: 1.040, Paradigm 3: 0.719.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Paradigm 3 showed a strong effect size for average freezing (Cohen's d: Paradigm 1: 0.797, Paradigm 2: 0.093, Paradigm 3: 1.232).
source: Average Freezing: Paradigm 1: 0.797, Paradigm 2: 0.093, Paradigm 3: 1.232).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Paradigm 1 produced the highest absolute freezing behavior in the CFC VR (average freezing: Paradigm 1: 23.54±3.26%, Paradigm 2: 21.51±4.21%, Paradigm 3: 21.92±2.95%).
source: On average, we found that Paradigm 1 still produced the highest absolute freezing behavior in the CFC VR (average freezing in all laps %: CFC VR: Paradigm 1: 23.54±3.26, Paradigm 2: 21.51±4.21, Paradigm 3: 21.92±2.95).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental data across paradigms.

claim: The difference in freezing behavior between the CFC VR and the neutral VR was comparable between Paradigms 1 and 3 (∆ average freezing %: Paradigm 1: 6.74, Paradigm 2: 0.61, Paradigm 3: 6.63).
source: The difference in freezing behavior between the CFC VR and the neutral VR was comparable between Paradigms 1 and 3 (∆ average freezing % (CFC VR – Familiar/Control VR): Paradigm 1: 6.74, Paradigm 2: 0.61, Paradigm 3: 6.63).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental data across paradigms.

claim: In Paradigm 3, mice maintained their ability to discriminate between the two VRs for the first two recall days.
source: Mice also maintained their ability to discriminate between the two VRs for the first two recall days, freezing significantly more in the CFC VR than in the Control VR on both Recall Days 1 and 2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: In Paradigm 3, by Recall Day 3, discrimination diminished as freezing levels no longer differed significantly between the two VRs.
source: However, by Recall Day 3, this discrimination diminished, as freezing levels no longer differed significantly between the two VRs.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental data across recall days.

claim: In Paradigm 3, mice showed delayed extinction compared to Paradigm 2.
source: Unlike the rapid fear extinction observed in Paradigm 2, mice in Paradigm 3 showed delayed extinction (Tables 5–6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Tables 5–6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: In Paradigm 3, freezing levels in the CFC VR remained elevated above baseline during the first lap and across all laps on Recall Days 1 and 2.
source: Freezing levels in the CFC VR remained elevated above baseline during the first lap and across all laps on Recall Days 1 and 2, with average freezing still elevated above baseline on Recall Day 3.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis using Linear Mixed Effects Model (Tables 5–6).

claim: The hippocampus plays a critical role in the encoding, consolidation, and recall of memories.
source: The hippocampus plays a critical role in the encoding, consolidation, and recall of memories and is necessary for the expression of contextual fear memory (Anagnostaras et al., 2001; Ji and Maren, 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Maren et al., 2013; Maren and Holt, 2000; Phillips and LeDoux, 1992; Ramirez et al., 2013; Wiltgen and Silva, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The hippocampus is necessary for the expression of contextual fear memory.
source: The hippocampus plays a critical role in the encoding, consolidation, and recall of memories and is necessary for the expression of contextual fear memory (Anagnostaras et al., 2001; Ji and Maren, 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Maren et al., 2013; Maren and Holt, 2000; Phillips and LeDoux, 1992; Ramirez et al., 2013; Wiltgen and Silva, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Context is thought to be represented in the hippocampus by place cells that fire at specific spatial locations (place fields) in an environment.
source: Context is thought to be represented in the hippocampus by place cells that fire at specific spatial locations (place fields) in an environment (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to foundational work on place cells.

claim: Previous studies on freely moving animals have shown that fear conditioning can cause place cells to remap.
source: Previous studies on freely moving animals have shown that fear conditioning can cause place cells to remap (Blair et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2015; Kinsky et al., 2023; Mamad et al., 2019; Moita et al., 2004; Ormond et al., 2023; Schuette et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Remapping is defined by place cells shifting their firing fields, indicative of place cells adapting to incorporate new information into memory.
source: Remapping is defined by place cells shifting their firing fields, indicative of place cells adapting to incorporate new information into memory (Colgin et al., 2008; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Muller and Kubie, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A recent study found that fear conditioning narrows the width of place fields in the feared environment in freely moving mice.
source: Additionally, a recent study (Schuette et al., 2020) that performed calcium imaging of hippocampal cells in freely moving mice found that fear conditioning narrows the width of place fields in the feared environment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a specific prior study.

claim: Narrower place fields suggest that place cells encode the same environment on a finer scale following fear conditioning, potentially enhancing context discrimination and threat avoidance.
source: This suggests that place cells encode the same environment on a finer scale following fear conditioning, potentially enhancing context discrimination and threat avoidance (Schuette et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and represents an interpretation of prior findings.

claim: A subset of place cells formed before CFC remained stable, while others remapped or changed their preferred firing locations after CFC.
source: We found that a subset of place cells formed before CFC remained stable, while others remapped or changed their preferred firing locations after CFC (see examples in Figure 7C and D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C and D–G.

claim: Place cell remapping after CFC is similar to previously reported observations in freely moving animals.
source: This is similar to previously reported observations (Blair et al., 2023; Moita et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Remapping occurred in both the Familiar and the CFC VR to similar extents.
source: We found remapping to occur in both the Familiar and the CFC VR to similar extents, as indicated by the lower correlation across sessions/days compared to the within-session correlation (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7F–G.

claim: There was an increase in the number of place cells in the CFC VR during memory recall.
source: Interestingly, we found an increase in the number of place cells in the CFC VR during memory recall, a finding not previously reported (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A–B.

claim: Place cells had narrower fields in the CFC VR during memory recall.
source: We also found that place cells had narrower fields in the CFC VR during memory recall (Figure 8C), as previously shown (Schuette et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C and citation to prior work.

claim: No significant difference was found in lap-by-lap reliability and out-of-field firing of place cells.
source: We did not find a significant difference in other place cell parameters we examined, such as lap-by-lap reliability (Figure 8D) and out-of-field firing (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8D and 8E.

claim: Head-fixed mice exhibited freezing behavior in response to an aversive stimulus in VR, consistent with conditioned responses seen in freely moving animals.
source: Our key findings are: (1) Head-fixed mice exhibited freezing behavior in response to an aversive stimulus in VR, consistent with conditioned responses seen in freely moving animals.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding of the study, supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Freezing was especially pronounced during the first lap in the fear-conditioned environment compared to the neutral environment across all paradigms tested.
source: Freezing was especially pronounced during the first lap in the fear-conditioned environment compared to the neutral environment across all paradigms tested.
evidence: The claim summarizes a consistent finding across all three paradigms, supported by data in Figures 2-6.

claim: Additional conditioned responses such as hesitation and backward movement were detected on the cylindrical treadmill.
source: (2) With mice on a cylindrical treadmill, additional conditioned responses such as hesitation and backward movement were detected.
evidence: The claim summarizes observed behaviors, supported by data and videos in the manuscript.

claim: Mice froze more in the fear-conditioned VR when the neutral environment was familiar rather than novel.
source: (3) The choice of neutral environment influenced fear discrimination: mice froze more in the fear-conditioned VR when the neutral environment was familiar rather than novel.
evidence: The claim summarizes a comparison between paradigms, supported by data in Figures 2-6.

claim: Freezing in the fear-conditioned VR could be enhanced by shorter ISIs and the presence of the tail-coat during recall when the neutral environment was novel.
source: Freezing in the fear-conditioned VR could be enhanced by shorter ISIs and the presence of the tail-coat during recall when the neutral environment was novel.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from Paradigm 3, supported by data in Figures 5-6.

claim: Following fear conditioning, place cells in the hippocampal CA1 region showed remapping, increased numbers, and narrower fields.
source: (4) Following fear conditioning, place cells in the hippocampal CA1 region showed remapping, increased numbers, and narrower fields, paralleling findings in freely moving animals and offering new insights.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from the imaging experiments, supported by data in Figures 7-8.

claim: A mild electric shock applied to the tail could trigger freezing behavior as the conditioned response in head-fixed mice.
source: In our study, we found that a mild electric shock applied to the tail could also trigger freezing behavior as the conditioned response in head-fixed mice, making our paradigm more comparable to the freely moving paradigms than previously attempted methods using air-puff stimulation (Lovett-Barron et al., 2014; Rajasethupathy et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by data throughout the manuscript and citations to prior work.

claim: The head-fixed setup allows for easy measurement of physiological responses including pupil diameter, respiration, vocalization, heart rate, and body temperature.
source: The head-fixed setup allows us to easily measure physiological responses including pupil diameter, respiration, vocalization, heart rate, and body temperature.
evidence: The claim describes capabilities of the experimental setup.

claim: Physiological parameters are known to change with fear conditioning.
source: These parameters are known to change with fear conditioning (Dupin et al., 2020; Godsil et al., 2000; Korn et al., 2017; Shionoya et al., 2013; Stiedl and Spiess, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Engram cells are identified based on the expression of the immediate early gene Fos during fear conditioning.
source: Typically, these cells are identified based on the expression of the immediate early gene Fos during fear conditioning.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge in the field of memory engrams.

claim: Artificial activation of engram cells with optogenetics can trigger memory recall, evidenced by increased freezing behavior.
source: Their artificial activation with optogenetics can trigger memory recall, evidenced by increased freezing behavior.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge in the field of memory engrams.

claim: A recent study revealed that cells forming engrams were inherently more active.
source: For instance, a recent study (Monasterio et al., 2024) tagged engram cells during fear conditioning while animals were freely moving and then imaged the spontaneous dynamics of these cells using two-photon imaging before and after fear conditioning. The study revealed that cells forming engrams were inherently more active.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a specific prior study.

claim: Fields of view during shock and subsequent flight-like response periods remained stable and could be corrected with Suite2p.
source: Our fields of view during the shock and subsequent flight-like response periods remained stable, and we could correct image movements during these periods with Suite2p (Pachitariu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim describes technical capabilities of the imaging approach used in the study.

claim: In Paradigm 1 imaging experiments, no cells were found responding to the shock itself.
source: In Paradigm 1, where we imaged hippocampal cells during shock, we did not find cells responding to the shock itself, as others have reported (Barth et al., 2023; Mocle et al., 2024; Suthard et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of imaging data and comparison to prior work.

claim: The head-fixed CFC paradigm is less naturalistic compared to freely moving CFC.
source: Compared to the freely moving CFC, our setup is less naturalistic.
evidence: The claim represents an acknowledged limitation of the approach.

claim: Different contexts were defined as two visually distinct VR environments while odor, sound, and tactile cues remained constant.
source: We defined different contexts as two visually distinct VR environments while odor, sound, and tactile cues remained constant.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design.

claim: Mice were water-restricted throughout the experimental process.
source: Unlike freely moving animals in CFC studies, our mice were water-restricted throughout the experimental process.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The criterion for advancement excludes mice that are less adept at running, limiting the number that go through the process and requiring larger cohorts of mice.
source: This criterion excludes mice that are less adept at running, limiting the number that go through the process and requiring larger cohorts of mice.
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: Only some female mice reached the experimental stage.
source: Furthermore, despite our best efforts to include equal numbers of male and female mice, only some female mice reached the experimental stage.
evidence: The claim describes an observed limitation in the study.

claim: Female mice of the same age (10–12 wk) weighed significantly less than males (20–23 g vs 25–30 g) and lost further weight following water restriction.
source: Female mice of the same age (10–12 wk) weighed significantly less than males (20–23 g vs 25–30 g) and lost further weight following water restriction.
evidence: The claim is based on observed data about mouse weights.

claim: No behavioral differences were observed between the four tested females and the male mice.
source: Although we observed no behavioral differences between the four tested females and the male mice, we cannot guarantee similar results in other female animals without further testing.
evidence: The claim is based on observed data from the study.

claim: Studies indicate that different sexes may display varying conditioned responses in rats.
source: Studies indicate that different sexes may display varying conditioned responses, as seen in rats (Gruene et al., 2015; Maren et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.
